name: Betahistine Dihydrochloride
sections: White crystalline hygroscopic powder (dihydrochloride), very soluble in water.

Widely used in Europe and Asia for Ménière's disease; the BEMED trial (2016) found no superiority over placebo for reducing attack frequency. First approval/introduction: Registered in Europe 1970 for Ménière's disease; US FDA 1966 approval withdrawn 1972.

Weak H1 agonist and potent H3 antagonist; increases inner-ear microcirculation and reduces endolymphatic pressure, and modulates vestibular nuclei activity, promoting vestibular compensation. Receptor / target profile: Weak partial H1 agonist and potent H3 antagonist/inverse agonist; increases inner-ear and vestibular blood flow and histamine release in brainstem.
Summary: Rapidly and almost completely absorbed; metabolised to inactive 2-pyridylacetic acid. Half-life ~3.5 h. Excreted in urine.
Adults: 24–48 mg/day in divided doses (16 mg three times daily or 24 mg twice daily)
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Urticaria, rash, allergic rhinitis may be aggravated
Nausea, somnolence, abdominal pain; seizures with very high doses. Supportive care.
BEMED (Adrion et al., BMJ 2016) – high-dose betahistine did not reduce Ménière's attacks versus placebo.
Older trials and meta-analyses suggest symptomatic benefit in vestibular vertigo.
Take with meals to avoid stomach upset
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
